cards.q: How is warfarin-associated ICH with INR 2 or more reversed?
cards.a: 4F-PCC (25 to 50 IU/kg by INR and weight, or fixed 1,500 U) plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV.

cards.q: What is the dabigatran reversal agent and dose?
cards.a: Idarucizumab 5 g IV, given as two 2.5 g boluses.

cards.q: What happened to andexanet alfa in the US in December 2025?
cards.a: It was withdrawn from the US market (effective December 22, 2025) over thromboembolic risk; 4F-PCC is the practical factor Xa reversal option.

cards.q: Should patients on aspirin with ICH and no planned surgery receive platelets?
cards.a: No; platelet transfusion is potentially harmful in that setting.

concepts.s: Treat any seizure lasting 5 minutes as status epilepticus with a full-dose benzodiazepine, then a second-line load of levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate by 20 minutes, then anesthetic infusions for refractory seizures.

x.b:
• Convulsive status epilepticus: continuous seizure of 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without return to baseline.
  • Nonconvulsive status should be suspected when consciousness does not recover after convulsions stop, or after paralysis for intubation.
  • Causes to hunt: low antiseizure drug levels, alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, toxins (isoniazid, tricyclics, bupropion, sympathomimetics), CNS infection, stroke, hemorrhage, trauma, eclampsia.

• Fingerstick glucose immediately; electrolytes including sodium, calcium, magnesium; antiseizure drug levels; toxicology; pregnancy test; CBC.
  • CT head once stabilized; LP when infection is possible; EEG when the patient does not return to baseline.

Timing and first-line doses follow the 2016 American Epilepsy Society guideline; second-line doses are the ESETT doses tabulated in the 2024 ACEP clinical policy on seizures.

  1. 0 to 5 minutes, stabilize: airway, oxygen, glucose check, cardiac monitoring, IV access; thiamine in adults.
  2. 5 to 20 minutes, benzodiazepine (Level A): midazolam IM 10 mg if over 40 kg (5 mg for 13 to 40 kg); or lorazepam IV 0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg per dose; or diazepam IV 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg, maximum 10 mg per dose (University of Maryland EM pearl). One repeat dose is permissible. IV phenobarbital if none is available.
  3. 20 to 40 minutes, second-line load (ACEP 2024 Level A: similar efficacy, about half stop): levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4,500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV (maximum 1,500 mg PE), avoid with AV block or sinus bradycardia; or valproate 40 mg/kg IV (maximum 3,000 mg), avoid in hepatic disease. ESETT infused each over 10 minutes.
  4. 40 to 60 minutes, refractory status: intubate and start a continuous infusion titrated to cessation of electrographic seizures or burst suppression, with continuous EEG (2012 Neurocritical Care Society guideline). Doses from a University of Maryland EM review that cites that guideline: midazolam 0.2 mg/kg load, then 0.05 to 2 mg/kg/h; propofol 1 to 2 mg/kg load, then 20 to 200 mcg/kg/min (watch for propofol infusion syndrome); pentobarbital 5 mg/kg load, then 0.5 to 5 mg/kg/h; ketamine 0.5 to 3 mg/kg load, then 1.5 to 10 mg/kg/h. No agent is proven superior.
  5. Eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4 to 6 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 to 2 g/h; without IV access, 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock). For recurrent seizures, lorazepam 2 to 4 mg IV (repeatable once). Doses from the ACOG District II Safe Motherhood Initiative eclampsia algorithm (2019). Obtain obstetric consultation.

Trap: Underdosing the benzodiazepine, such as 1 to 2 mg of lorazepam in an adult. ESETT required adequate prior doses (diazepam 10 mg, lorazepam 4 mg, or midazolam 10 mg, or weight-based equivalents) before calling seizures benzodiazepine refractory.
  • Waiting for IV access delays treatment; IM midazolam works as well as IV lorazepam.
  • After paralysis, a still patient may still be seizing; get EEG.
  • Isoniazid toxicity needs pyridoxine; hyponatremic seizures need hypertonic saline; these do not respond reliably to standard antiseizure drugs.
  • Refractory status and anyone intubated go to ICU with continuous EEG.

cards.q: What is the IM midazolam dose for status epilepticus in a patient over 40 kg?
cards.a: 10 mg IM (5 mg for 13 to 40 kg).

cards.q: What is the IV lorazepam dose for status epilepticus?
cards.a: 0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg per dose, repeatable once.

cards.q: What are the ESETT second-line doses and maxima?
cards.a: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4,500 mg); fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg (max 1,500 mg PE); valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3,000 mg).

cards.q: What magnesium regimen treats eclamptic seizures?
cards.a: Magnesium sulfate 4 to 6 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 to 2 g/h; 10 g IM (5 g each buttock) if no IV access.

cards.q: At what time point does the AES timeline move to second-line therapy?
cards.a: About 20 minutes after seizure onset if benzodiazepines fail.

concepts.n: Subarachnoid hemorrhage and headache red flags
concepts.s: A sudden headache peaking within an hour needs the Ottawa SAH rule, and a normal noncontrast CT within 6 hours of onset in a neurologically intact patient rules out SAH.

x.b:
• Headache red flags: thunderclap onset, onset during exertion, syncope or witnessed loss of consciousness, neck pain or stiffness, focal deficit, papilledema, new headache over age 50, fever, immunosuppression or cancer, pregnancy or postpartum, anticoagulation, positional or Valsalva-triggered pain.
  • Thunderclap differential: aneurysmal SAH, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, cerebral venous thrombosis, cervical artery dissection, pituitary apoplexy, ICH, hypertensive emergency.

c.b:
Applies to alert patients over 15 with a new, severe, nontraumatic headache reaching maximum intensity within 1 hour. Exclude new neurologic deficits, prior aneurysm, SAH or brain tumor, and recurrent similar headaches (3 or more over 6 months). Investigate if any are present:

  • Age 40 or older
  • Neck pain or stiffness
  • Witnessed loss of consciousness
  • Onset during exertion
  • Thunderclap (instantly peaking) headache
  • Limited neck flexion on exam

The six-item rule had 100% sensitivity in its derivation work with low specificity; ACEP 2019 endorses it (Level B).

x.b:
• Noncontrast CT within 6 hours of onset (third-generation scanner or newer), normal in a patient with a normal neurologic exam, rules out nontraumatic SAH without LP (ACEP 2019 Level B; the 2023 AHA/ASA aSAH guideline cites 99% sensitivity).
  • After 6 hours with a negative CT: LP (the 2023 AHA/ASA guideline) or CTA as a reasonable alternative chosen with shared decision making (ACEP Level C). CTA finds incidental aneurysms; LP has traumatic taps.
  • Positive CT: CTA to find the aneurysm; DSA when hemorrhage is diffuse and CTA is negative.
  • Grade with Hunt and Hess or WFNS for communication and prognosis.

From the 2023 AHA/ASA aneurysmal SAH guideline (as summarized in AFP) and drug dosing summarized in US Pharmacist.

  • Blood pressure: keep SBP at 160 mm Hg or less before the aneurysm is secured, avoiding hypotension and variability; use titratable IV agents.
  • Reverse anticoagulation as for ICH.
  • Nimodipine 60 mg PO or via tube every 4 hours for 21 days, started early; if it drops BP, give 30 mg every 2 hours.
  • Secure the aneurysm (coiling or clipping) within 24 hours when feasible.
  • Hydrocephalus: external ventricular drain.
  • Seizures: consider prophylaxis only for high-risk features (high-grade SAH, hydrocephalus, cortical infarction, intracerebral hemorrhage, MCA aneurysm, per AFP); continuing after a presenting seizure for up to 7 days is reasonable; avoid phenytoin.
  • Maintain euvolemia. TXA does not improve outcome and is not recommended.

Trap: Diagnosing migraine in a first or worst headache with abrupt onset. A sentinel bleed can resolve and look benign hours before a catastrophic rupture.
  • CT sensitivity falls with time after onset; the 6-hour rule depends on a modern scanner and an experienced reader.
  • Delayed cerebral ischemia affects about 30% of patients, typically days 4 to 14.
  • All SAH patients go to a neuro ICU at a center with neurosurgery and neurointerventional capability; transfer early.
  • For primary headache treatment, ACEP prefers nonopioid therapy (Level A).

cards.q: List the six Ottawa SAH rule variables.
cards.a: Age 40 or older, neck pain or stiffness, witnessed loss of consciousness, onset during exertion, thunderclap onset, limited neck flexion.

cards.q: When does a normal noncontrast CT rule out SAH without LP per ACEP 2019?
cards.a: When done within 6 hours of headache onset in a patient with a normal neurologic exam.

cards.q: What is the nimodipine regimen in aneurysmal SAH?
cards.a: 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days (30 mg every 2 hours if hypotension occurs).

cards.q: What SBP limit does the 2023 AHA/ASA guideline use before the aneurysm is secured?
cards.a: 160 mm Hg or less, avoiding hypotension and variability.

cards.q: Name four causes of thunderclap headache besides aneurysmal SAH.
cards.a: RCVS, cerebral venous thrombosis, cervical artery dissection, pituitary apoplexy (also ICH, hypertensive emergency).

concepts.n: Trauma primary survey and hemorrhagic shock
concepts.s: Stop bleeding first, resuscitate with whole blood or balanced components instead of crystalloid, give TXA within 3 hours, and move the patient to definitive hemorrhage control.

x.b:
• ATLS 11th edition primary survey: x exsanguinating hemorrhage, A airway with cervical spine protection, B breathing, C circulation, D disability, E exposure and temperature.
  • Where blood is lost: external, chest, abdomen, pelvis and retroperitoneum, long bones.
  • Shock signs: tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, cool skin, delayed capillary refill, confusion. Hypotension is a late sign; older and beta-blocked patients may not become tachycardic.
  • ABC score (ACS TQIP): 1 point each for HR over 120, SBP under 90, positive FAST, penetrating torso injury; 2 or more triggers massive transfusion.

• eFAST (pericardium, abdomen, chest), chest and pelvis X-ray in the bay.
  • Type and crossmatch, CBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, VBG with lactate and base deficit, ionized calcium; viscoelastic testing (TEG or ROTEM) to guide products where available.
  • CT only when the patient is stable enough to leave the resuscitation bay.

1. External hemorrhage control: direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquets, pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture (ATLS 11).
  2. Minimize crystalloid; use it only as a bridge until blood is available (ATLS 11).
  3. Blood: ATLS 11 prefers low-titer O whole blood when available, otherwise balanced 1:1:1 plasma, platelets, and red cells. The 2014 ACS TQIP guideline gives plasma to red cells of 1:1 to 1:2 and one platelet pool per 6 units of red cells, with coolers every 15 minutes.
  4. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours (ACS TQIP; ATLS 11). ATLS 11 also supports a 2 g bolus in TBI.
  5. Permissive hypotension until hemorrhage is controlled (ATLS 11), except with TBI, where SBP should stay above 100 to 110 depending on age.
  6. Calcium: citrate in transfused blood lowers ionized calcium; the ACS TQIP guideline lists ionized calcium as a monitored value and hypocalcemia as a target for correction but gives no dose (confirm dose in a current reference).
  7. Definitive control: operating room, angioembolization, or preperitoneal packing; activate early.

Trap: A negative FAST read as "no bleeding." FAST misses retroperitoneal and pelvic hemorrhage and small volumes; an unstable patient with a negative FAST still needs a source found.
  • Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy reinforce each other; warm all fluids and the room, and limit crystalloid.
  • Starting TXA after 3 hours is outside the evidence window.
  • TQIP termination guide values once bleeding is controlled include hemoglobin 10 g/dL or more, PT under 18 s, aPTT under 35 s, platelets over 150,000, and fibrinogen over 180 mg/dL.
  • Transfer early when the facility cannot provide surgery, interventional radiology, or blood products at scale.

cards.q: What are the four elements of the ABC score for massive transfusion?
cards.a: HR over 120, SBP under 90, positive FAST, penetrating torso injury; 2 or more activates MTP.

cards.q: What is the trauma TXA regimen and window?
cards.a: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours of injury.

cards.q: What does ATLS 11 prefer for hemorrhagic shock resuscitation when available?
cards.a: Low-titer O whole blood; otherwise balanced 1:1:1 components with minimal crystalloid.

cards.q: What platelet ratio does the ACS TQIP massive transfusion guideline use?
cards.a: One apheresis or pooled platelet unit for every 6 units of red cells.

cards.q: Why is permissive hypotension avoided in TBI?
cards.a: Hypotension worsens secondary brain injury; ATLS 11 targets SBP above 100 to 110 depending on age.

concepts.n: Traumatic brain injury and head CT decision rules
concepts.s: Use the Canadian CT Head Rule for adults with minor head injury and PECARN for children, and in severe TBI prevent secondary injury by avoiding hypotension, hypoxia, and hyperventilation.

x.b:
• Mild TBI is GCS 13 to 15; moderate 9 to 12; severe 8 or less.
  • Herniation signs: unilateral fixed dilated pupil, extensor posturing, declining GCS, Cushing response (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing).
  • Anticoagulated and older patients bleed after trivial mechanisms.
The 2023 ACEP mild TBI clinical policy recommends the Canadian CT Head Rule (Level A); the NEXUS Head CT instrument (NEXUS II) and the New Orleans Criteria are acceptable but less specific (Level B).

c.b:
For GCS 13 to 15 with loss of consciousness, amnesia, or witnessed disorientation. Not for age under 16, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, or post-traumatic seizure.

  • High risk (neurosurgical lesion): GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF leak), 2 or more episodes of vomiting, age 65 or older.
  • Medium risk (brain injury on CT): retrograde amnesia over 30 minutes; dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck, ejection, fall from more than 3 feet or 5 stairs).

• Under 2 years, CT if: GCS 14 or less, altered mental status, palpable skull fracture. Consider CT or observation if: non-frontal scalp hematoma, loss of consciousness 5 seconds or more, severe mechanism, not acting normally per parent.
  • 2 years and older, CT if: GCS 14 or less, altered mental status, signs of basilar skull fracture. Consider CT or observation if: vomiting, loss of consciousness, severe mechanism, severe headache.

Immediate CT after mild TBI. Routine observation or repeat CT is not recommended when initial CT and neurologic exam are normal; observation may be considered for older patients on antiplatelets with loss of consciousness, amnesia, or GCS under 15.

x.b:
Severe TBI targets from the Brain Trauma Foundation 4th edition and ACS TQIP, with ATLS 11 updates.

  • Blood pressure: SBP 100 or more for ages 50 to 69 and 110 or more for ages 15 to 49 and over 70 (BTF Level III); ATLS 11 similarly targets SBP above 100 to 110 by age.
  • Oxygenation and ventilation: avoid hypoxia (TQIP SpO2 over 95%), PaCO2 35 to 45 mm Hg; no prolonged prophylactic hyperventilation to PaCO2 25 or less.
  • ICP and CPP: treat ICP over 22 mm Hg; CPP 60 to 70 mm Hg.
  • Herniation: head of bed up, brief hyperventilation only as a bridge, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.25 to 1 g/kg per older BTF guidance while avoiding hypotension, or hypertonic saline; confirm hypertonic saline dose in a current reference), emergency neurosurgery.
  • Reverse anticoagulation immediately (see ICH concept); TQIP targets INR under 1.4 and platelets over 75,000.
  • Seizure prophylaxis for 7 days reduces early post-traumatic seizures (BTF names phenytoin; levetiracetam is widely used with insufficient evidence to favor either).
  • No steroids (Level I: high-dose methylprednisolone increased mortality).
  • TXA: ATLS 11 supports a 2 g bolus in TBI within 3 hours.

Trap: Applying the Canadian CT Head Rule to patients it excluded, such as anticoagulated patients or those with a post-traumatic seizure. Those patients need CT.
  • Intoxication confounds GCS; image if the exam cannot be trusted.
  • Discharge after a normal CT with strict return precautions and follow-up; ACEP does not recommend routine repeat CT for normal initial imaging and exam.
  • Any intracranial bleed, depressed GCS, or anticoagulant-associated injury needs neurosurgical consultation and admission.

cards.q: List the five high-risk Canadian CT Head Rule criteria.
cards.a: GCS under 15 at 2 hours, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, signs of basilar skull fracture, 2 or more vomiting episodes, age 65 or older.

cards.q: Which patients are excluded from the Canadian CT Head Rule?
cards.a: Age under 16, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and post-traumatic seizure.

cards.q: What SBP targets does the Brain Trauma Foundation give by age?
cards.a: 100 or more for ages 50 to 69; 110 or more for ages 15 to 49 and over 70.

cards.q: What are the PECARN high-risk criteria in a child under 2?
cards.a: GCS 14 or less, altered mental status, or palpable skull fracture.

cards.q: At what ICP does the BTF recommend treatment?
cards.a: Over 22 mm Hg.

concepts.s: Clear the cervical spine clinically with NEXUS or the more sensitive Canadian C-spine Rule in alert stable adults, image with CT when the rules fail, and restrict spinal motion selectively.

x.b:
• Neck pain or tenderness after a mechanism capable of spinal injury; paresthesias or weakness; priapism or neurogenic shock (hypotension with bradycardia) in cord injury.
  • Older adults fracture after ground-level falls, often at C1 and C2; hyperextension injuries cause central cord syndrome (arms weaker than legs).
Apply each rule only to the population it was derived in.

c.t: NEXUS low-risk criteria (all 5 needed to skip imaging)
c.b:
• No posterior midline cervical tenderness
  • No focal neurologic deficit
  • Normal alertness
  • No intoxication
  • No painful distracting injury

c.t: Canadian C-spine Rule (alert GCS 15, stable adults)
c.b:
1. Any high-risk factor means image: age 65 or older; dangerous mechanism (fall from 3 feet or 5 stairs, axial load, high-speed or rollover crash or ejection, motorized recreational vehicle, bicycle collision); paresthesias in the extremities.
  2. Any low-risk factor that allows range-of-motion testing: simple rear-end collision, sitting in the ED, ambulatory at any time, delayed onset of neck pain, no midline tenderness. No low-risk factor means image.
  3. Can actively rotate 45 degrees left and right: no imaging. Cannot: image.

In Stiell's 2003 NEJM comparison of 8,282 patients, CCR sensitivity was 99.4% versus 90.7% for NEXUS, with higher specificity (40.4% vs 33.0%).
CT is the adult imaging test of choice when a rule fails. MRI for neurologic deficits, suspected ligamentous or cord injury, or symptoms out of proportion to a normal CT.

x.b:
• ATLS 11th edition makes spinal motion restriction selective and criteria based, with less reliance on rigid collars, especially in penetrating trauma.
  • Neurogenic shock: exclude hemorrhage first, then treat with vasopressors and atropine or pacing for bradycardia (confirm MAP goals and doses with spine surgery and current references).
  • Spine surgery consultation for fractures, ligamentous injury, or cord findings.

Trap: Using the Canadian C-spine Rule outside its population: GCS under 15, unstable vitals, age under 16, acute paralysis, penetrating neck trauma, pregnancy, or known vertebral disease. Those patients need imaging or a different pathway.
  • NEXUS depends on judgment about intoxication and distracting injury; uncertainty means the patient is not low risk.
  • Collars cause pressure injury, airway difficulty, and raised ICP; remove them once the spine is cleared.
  • Older patients with a fracture need admission for pain, swallowing, and fall evaluation even when the fracture is stable.

cards.q: List the five NEXUS low-risk criteria.
cards.a: No midline cervical tenderness, no focal deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, no painful distracting injury.

cards.q: What are the three Canadian C-spine Rule high-risk factors?
cards.a: Age 65 or older, dangerous mechanism, paresthesias in the extremities.

cards.q: What is the final step of the Canadian C-spine Rule?
cards.a: Ask the patient to actively rotate the neck 45 degrees left and right; inability means image.

cards.q: How did CCR compare with NEXUS in Stiell 2003?
cards.a: CCR sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7% for NEXUS, with higher specificity.

cards.q: How does ATLS 11 change spinal motion restriction?
cards.a: It is selective and criteria based, with less use of rigid collars, especially in penetrating trauma.

concepts.s: Estimate burned area from partial- and full-thickness burns only, protect the airway early when inhalation injury is likely, start lactated Ringer's at 2 mL/kg per %TBSA for adults over 20% TBSA titrated to urine output, and consult a burn center early.

x.b:
• Depth: superficial (red, painful, no blisters; not counted in TBSA); partial thickness (blisters, moist, painful); full thickness (leathery, white or charred, insensate).
  • TBSA: rule of nines in adults; the patient's palm with fingers is about 1%; Lund-Browder charts for children.
  • Inhalation injury indicators (burn center pocket guide): enclosed-space fire, facial burns, singed eyebrows or nasal hair, soot in the mouth or pharynx, hoarseness, stridor, inability to clear secretions, altered mental status.
  • Look for associated trauma, carbon monoxide and cyanide toxicity, circumferential burns, and non-accidental injury in children.

• Carboxyhemoglobin, lactate (high lactate suggests cyanide), blood gas, CBC, chemistry.
  • Electrical injury: ECG, CK, urinalysis for myoglobin.
  • Secondary survey for trauma from blasts, falls, or escape.

1. Stop the burning process and remove clothing and jewelry.
  2. Airway: 100% oxygen; intubate early for stridor, hoarseness, or progressive edema. Secure the tube with ties, not tape, over facial burns.
  3. Fluids for partial- and full-thickness burns over 20% TBSA (burn center pocket guide following ABLS conventions): lactated Ringer's 2 mL x kg x %TBSA for adults, 3 mL for children under 13, 4 mL for electrical injury, over 24 hours from the time of injury. The initial hourly rate is that total divided by 16 (half in the first 8 hours).
  4. Titrate to urine output, adjusting the rate by about one third each hour: adults 30 to 50 mL/h, children under 30 kg 1 mL/kg/h, high-voltage electrical injury 75 to 100 mL/h. Place a urinary catheter for burns over 20% TBSA.
  5. Cyanide (smoke inhalation with shock or high lactate): hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes; a second 5 g may be given over 15 minutes (in extremis) to 2 hours, total 10 g, per the Cyanokit FDA label.
  6. Escharotomy for circumferential chest burns impairing ventilation or limb burns threatening perfusion, in consultation with the burn center.
  7. Analgesia, warming, tetanus prophylaxis, clean dry dressings.

Trap: Counting superficial (first-degree) burns in TBSA, which inflates the fluid calculation and drives over-resuscitation (fluid creep), compartment syndromes, and pulmonary edema.
  • Calculate from the time of injury, not arrival; delayed starts need catch-up.
  • Normal SpO2 does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.
  • American Burn Association criteria for immediate consultation and consideration of transfer: full-thickness burns; partial-thickness burns of 10% TBSA or more; deep burns of the face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, or major joints; burns in patients with significant comorbidity or concurrent trauma; poorly controlled pain; all suspected inhalation injury; high-voltage (1,000 V or more) electrical and lightning injury; all chemical injuries. The 2026 burn center pocket guide's list also includes radiation injury and frostbite. Children may benefit from referral for pain, dressing, rehabilitation, or safeguarding needs.

cards.q: What fluid formula do current ABLS-style protocols use for adult burns over 20% TBSA?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's 2 mL x kg x %TBSA over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from time of injury (3 mL for children, 4 mL for electrical).

cards.q: What urine output targets guide burn resuscitation?
cards.a: Adults 30 to 50 mL/h; children under 30 kg 1 mL/kg/h; high-voltage electrical 75 to 100 mL/h.

cards.q: Which burns are excluded from TBSA calculation?
cards.a: Superficial (first-degree) burns.

cards.q: What is the hydroxocobalamin dose for cyanide toxicity in smoke inhalation?
cards.a: 5 g IV over 15 minutes, with a second 5 g dose over 15 minutes to 2 hours if needed (total 10 g), per the Cyanokit label.

cards.q: Name four ABA criteria for immediate burn center consultation.
cards.a: Full-thickness burns, partial-thickness 10% TBSA or more, deep burns of face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, or joints, inhalation injury, high-voltage electrical, chemical injury (any four).

concepts.n: Accidental hypothermia and hypothermic cardiac arrest
concepts.s: Stage by core temperature and consciousness, handle gently, rewarm by stage, and send unstable or arrested patients to a center that can run ECLS because full neurologic recovery after hours of CPR is possible.

x.b:
The Wilderness Medical Society (WMS) 2019 hypothermia guideline uses core temperature bands: mild 35 to 32 C, moderate 32 to 28 C, severe below 28 C, with some experts adding profound below 24 C. When no thermometer is available, the Swiss staging maps clinical signs to risk: HT I conscious and shivering, HT II impaired consciousness without shivering, HT III unconscious, HT IV apparent death.

  • Clinical clues: shivering stops as temperature falls, confusion, bradycardia, slow respirations, cold diuresis, and eventually no detectable pulse.
  • A shivering patient with impaired consciousness should be treated as moderate (WMS).
  • VF risk rises sharply below 28 C, and rough handling can trigger it.
  • Must-not-miss contributors: hypoglycemia, sepsis, hypothyroidism (myxedema), adrenal insufficiency, head or spinal injury, intoxication, and in older adults an occult fall with a long lie.

• Core temperature: WMS recommends an esophageal probe in the lower third of the esophagus in intubated patients; rectal and bladder readings can lag core by up to an hour.
  • ECG: bradycardia, prolonged intervals, Osborn (J) waves, atrial fibrillation; shivering artifact is common.
  • Labs: glucose, potassium, blood gas, lactate, CK, coagulation (clotting assays run at 37 C underestimate the in-vivo coagulopathy), lipase, TSH and cortisol when the cause is unclear.
  • Potassium as a triage tool in arrest: WMS states CPR should be terminated in an adult with serum potassium above 12 mmol/L; with no ECLS available, take the arrested patient to the nearest hospital that can measure potassium and attempt conventional resuscitation if it is below 12.
  • Prognostic scores: the European Resuscitation Council (ERC) hypothermia algorithm suggests considering ECLS when the HOPE survival probability is 10 percent or higher.

1. Handle gently and keep horizontal. WMS links limb movement and upright posture to afterdrop (further core cooling of up to 5 to 6 C after rescue) and to circumrescue collapse.
  2. Rewarm by stage. Mild: insulation, warm environment, calories, shivering (about 3 to 4 C per hour per WMS). Moderate to severe: active external rewarming to the trunk (forced air, heat packs to axillae, chest, back), warm IV fluids, and in the hospital minimally invasive or invasive core rewarming. WMS cites a safe rewarming rate of 1 to 2 C per hour for noninvasive methods.
  3. Fluids: WMS recommends normal saline warmed to 40 to 42 C, given IV or IO as 500 mL boluses titrated to response, and advises against lactated Ringer's because the cold liver clears lactate poorly.
  4. Cardiac arrest: standard compressions; check for a pulse for up to 1 minute before starting CPR. If VF or pulseless VT and core is below 30 C, WMS recommends a single shock at maximum energy and delaying further shocks until the patient is warmer than 30 C. The 2025 European Resuscitation Council (ERC) guideline, as published by Resuscitation Council UK, instead delays further shocks only if VF persists after 3 shocks, until the core is above 30 C.
  5. Epinephrine: WMS recommends withholding vasoactive drugs until the core reaches 30 C, then giving usual doses with dosing intervals doubled between 30 and 35 C. The 2025 ERC guideline also withholds epinephrine below 30 C, then gives 1 mg IV once the core reaches 30 C (unless ECPR is about to start) and stretches the interval to 6 to 10 minutes between 30 and 35 C. Follow normothermic ACLS above 35 C.
  6. ECLS: WMS recommends transfer of arrested or hemodynamically unstable patients, and those below 28 C, to a center with ECLS; ECMO is preferred over cardiopulmonary bypass. ERC advises ECLS rewarming for HT IV and not terminating CPR during transport to ECLS.
  7. Drugs at low temperature: WMS advises reducing doses of anesthetic and neuromuscular blocking agents below 30 C.

Trap: Declaring death in a cold patient. WMS reports survival after 6.5 hours of CPR and after resuscitation from a core temperature of 13.7 C; there is no temperature cutoff below which resuscitation is futile.
  • Hypothermic arrest with a clear asphyxial cause (for example, burial without an air pocket, or submersion before cooling) has a worse outlook; potassium and HOPE help separate these cases.
  • Rewarming can unmask hypovolemia and cause hypotension; give warmed fluid and monitor.
  • Older patients found indoors are often hypothermic from an underlying illness; treat the cause.
  • Admit moderate or worse hypothermia; ICU for severe hypothermia, arrhythmia, or invasive rewarming.

Oxygen consumption falls about 6 percent per 1 C drop (to about 50 percent at 28 C per WMS), which protects the brain during prolonged arrest. The cold myocardium becomes irritable and poorly responsive to drugs and shocks, and enzymes slow, so drugs accumulate and coagulation fails.

cards.q: Per WMS 2019, when should epinephrine be withheld in hypothermic arrest, and how is dosing changed between 30 and 35 C?
cards.a: Withhold vasoactive drugs until core temperature reaches 30 C; between 30 and 35 C give usual doses at twice the usual interval (ERC 2025: 1 mg every 6 to 10 minutes).

cards.q: Per WMS 2019, what defibrillation strategy is used for VF below 30 C?
cards.a: One shock at maximum energy, then delay further shocks until the core is above 30 C (ERC 2025 allows up to 3 shocks before delaying).

cards.q: What serum potassium level does WMS 2019 give for terminating CPR in an adult hypothermic arrest?
cards.a: Above 12 mmol/L.

cards.q: Which IV fluid and temperature does WMS recommend for hypothermia?
cards.a: Normal saline warmed to 40 to 42 C in 500 mL boluses titrated to blood pressure; avoid lactated Ringer's.

cards.q: Define the core temperature bands for mild, moderate and severe hypothermia used by WMS.
cards.a: Mild 35 to 32 C, moderate 32 to 28 C, severe below 28 C.

concepts.s: Hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction is heat stroke until proven otherwise, and the treatment is immediate whole-body cold-water or ice-water immersion to below 39 C within 30 minutes.

x.b:
• Definition in practice: elevated core temperature (commonly above 40 C) with CNS dysfunction: confusion, ataxia, seizures, coma. Sweating may persist, especially in exertional heat stroke.
  • Exertional: young athletes, soldiers, laborers; rapid onset during exertion in heat.
  • Classic (nonexertional): older adults, chronic illness, anticholinergic or diuretic use, poor housing during heat waves; slower onset with more dehydration.
  • Differential: sepsis and meningitis, thyroid storm, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity, stroke involving the hypothalamus.

• Core temperature by rectal or esophageal probe, continuously during cooling. Oral, tympanic, and temporal readings are unreliable here.
  • Labs: glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, CK (rhabdomyolysis), LFTs (rise over 24 to 72 hours), coagulation and fibrinogen (DIC), lactate, blood gas, urinalysis.
  • Do not delay cooling for labs or imaging. Image the head or do an LP only if mental status fails to improve after cooling or the history suggests another cause.

1. Start cooling at the point of recognition. The 30-minute target below runs from recognition, so cool on site before transport whenever immersion is available. The 2025 Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) heat stroke guideline strongly recommends active over passive cooling and prioritizing the fastest available method: ice-water immersion (1 to 5 C) or cold-water immersion (9 to 12 C).
  2. Targets per SCCM 2025 (good practice statements): reach a core temperature below 39 C, within 30 minutes of recognition, using a method that cools at least 0.155 C per minute.
  3. When immersion is impossible: use the fastest alternative available (for example, ice packs over the body with cold wet sheets, or evaporative cooling with fanning), accepting slower rates.
  4. Stop at target to avoid overshoot hypothermia, then monitor for rebound.
  5. Supportive care: airway protection, benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering, isotonic fluids guided by perfusion and volume status (classic heat stroke patients are often older with cardiac disease), treat hypoglycemia, manage rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalemia.
  6. Do not use: SCCM 2025 strongly recommends against dantrolene and advises against routine acetaminophen, NSAIDs or salicylates for temperature reduction.

Trap: Treating the fever with antipyretics or slow external cooling while the patient sits at 41 C. Morbidity tracks the duration of hyperthermia, so immersion speed is the intervention.
  • A normal or near-normal temperature on arrival after prehospital cooling does not exclude heat stroke; the history and CNS findings define it.
  • Expect delayed liver injury, AKI, and DIC; admit all true heat stroke, with ICU for persistent CNS dysfunction, organ failure, or coagulopathy.
  • SCCM 2025 limits prophylactic antibiotics and antiseizure drugs to research settings.

Heat production or absorption overwhelms dissipation. Above a critical temperature, cells denature, the gut barrier leaks endotoxin, and a sepsis-like inflammatory and coagulation cascade follows, which is why damage continues after cooling and why time above 40 C matters most.

cards.q: What cooling method does the 2025 SCCM heat stroke guideline prioritize?
cards.a: The fastest available active method: ice-water (1 to 5 C) or cold-water (9 to 12 C) immersion.

cards.q: What temperature target and time window does SCCM 2025 give for heat stroke cooling?
cards.a: Core temperature below 39 C within 30 minutes of recognition.

cards.q: What minimum cooling rate does SCCM 2025 suggest prioritizing?
cards.a: At least 0.155 C per minute.

cards.q: Does SCCM 2025 support dantrolene or antipyretics in heat stroke?
cards.a: No; it strongly recommends against dantrolene and advises against routine antipyretics.

cards.q: Which thermometer site should guide heat stroke cooling?
cards.a: Continuous rectal or esophageal core temperature.

concepts.s: Diagnose with glucose or known diabetes, ketones, and acidosis (DKA) or extreme glucose and osmolality without major ketosis (HHS), then give fluids, check potassium before insulin, run fixed-rate insulin, and add dextrose before ketones clear.

x.b:
• DKA: polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration; develops over hours to a day.
  • HHS: older type 2 patients, days of osmotic diuresis, profound dehydration, altered mental status or focal deficits; mixed DKA/HHS is common.
  • Euglycemic DKA: the 2024 consensus defines it as glucose below 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with ketosis and acidosis, about 10 percent of presentations; SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, low intake, and alcohol are triggers.
  • Find the precipitant: insulin omission, infection, MI, stroke, pancreatitis, new diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors, steroids.

Diagnostic criteria per the 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus:

  • DKA (all three): glucose 200 mg/dL or higher or known diabetes; beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or higher (preferred) or urine ketones 2+ or more; pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L. Anion gap is no longer a primary criterion.
  • DKA severity: mild pH 7.25 to 7.30 or bicarbonate 15 to 18; moderate pH 7.0 to 7.25 or bicarbonate 10 to under 15; severe pH below 7.0 or bicarbonate below 10, or stupor or coma.
  • HHS (all four): glucose 600 mg/dL or higher; effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or total osmolality above 320; beta-hydroxybutyrate below 3.0 mmol/L or urine ketones below 2+; pH 7.3 or higher and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L or higher. Altered mental status is no longer required.
  • Also: potassium, sodium (correct for glucose), phosphate, creatinine, venous gas, CBC, lipase, ECG, cultures and imaging as indicated, pregnancy test.

1. Fluids: 0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid at 500 to 1000 mL/h for the first 2 to 4 hours if no cardiac or renal compromise, replacing the deficit over 24 to 48 hours. The consensus notes balanced crystalloids may resolve DKA faster with less hyperchloremia. Use smaller boluses (for example 250 mL) in older adults, heart failure, or kidney failure.
  2. Potassium before insulin: if K is below 3.5 mmol/L, hold insulin and replace at 10 mmol/h until K exceeds 3.5. If K is 3.5 to under 5.0, add 20 to 30 mmol per liter of fluid targeting 4 to 5. If K is 5.0 or higher, no initial replacement; recheck 2 hours after insulin starts, then every 4 hours.
  3. Insulin (DKA): IV fixed-rate 0.1 units/kg/h; an optional 0.1 units/kg IV or IM bolus if access is delayed. Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 1 to 2 hours is an alternative in mild to moderate uncomplicated DKA (not recommended for severe DKA or HHS).
  4. Dextrose: when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L), add 5 to 10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h, keeping glucose about 200 mg/dL until ketoacidosis resolves. In euglycemic DKA, start dextrose with the insulin.
  5. Insulin (HHS): 0.05 units/kg/h if ketosis is absent or mild; 0.1 units/kg/h if significant ketonemia (mixed picture). Fluids alone usually lower glucose first.
  6. HHS correction limits: glucose fall no faster than 90 to 120 mg/dL per hour; sodium fall no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours; osmolality fall 3 to 8 mOsm/kg per hour.
  7. Bicarbonate: not routine; consider only if pH is below 7.0: 100 mmol in 400 mL sterile water every 2 hours until pH exceeds 7.0.
  8. Phosphate: only with weakness, respiratory or cardiac compromise and phosphate below 1.0 mmol/L; 20 to 30 mmol potassium phosphate added to fluids.
  9. Resolution and transition: DKA resolves at ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher; HHS at osmolality below 300, glucose below 250 mg/dL, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h, and improved cognition. Overlap subcutaneous insulin with the drip by 1 to 2 hours before stopping it; the consensus also allows low-dose basal insulin (0.15 to 0.3 units/kg SC) to start while the infusion is still running. Starting doses are about 0.5 to 0.6 units/kg/day in insulin-naive patients, or 0.3 if hypoglycemia risk is high.

Trap: Starting insulin before the potassium is back. Insulin drives potassium into cells, and a patient with K below 3.5 can arrest from hypokalemia.
  • Stopping the insulin drip when glucose normalizes; the endpoint is ketone and acid clearance, so add dextrose and continue insulin.
  • Using the anion gap or urine ketones to judge resolution; the consensus advises against both.
  • Missing euglycemic DKA in a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor; stop the drug on admission.
  • Cerebral edema is rare in adults (under 0.1 percent) with about 30 percent mortality; correct HHS osmolality slowly and image for any mental status decline.
  • Disposition per the consensus: mild DKA ward or observation, moderate step-down, severe DKA and HHS in the ICU.

Insulin deficiency plus counter-regulatory hormones drive lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis (DKA) and gluconeogenesis with osmotic diuresis. In HHS, residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis, so the picture is dominated by water loss and hyperosmolality.

cards.q: What are the three DKA criteria in the 2024 consensus?
cards.a: Glucose 200 mg/dL or higher or known diabetes; beta-hydroxybutyrate 3.0 mmol/L or higher (or urine ketones 2+); pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18.

cards.q: What potassium level requires holding insulin in DKA?
cards.a: Below 3.5 mmol/L; replace at 10 mmol/h until K is above 3.5.

cards.q: What is the fixed-rate IV insulin dose for DKA, and what happens when glucose drops below 250 mg/dL?
cards.a: 0.1 units/kg/h; add 5 to 10% dextrose and reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/h.

cards.q: What are the 2024 DKA resolution criteria?
cards.a: Ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 mmol/L or higher.

cards.q: What sodium correction limit does the consensus give for HHS?
cards.a: No more than 10 mmol/L fall in 24 hours.

concepts.s: Check glucose in every altered patient, treat immediately with oral carbohydrate if able to swallow or IV dextrose or glucagon if not, then find the cause and decide how long it will recur.

x.b:
• ADA levels: level 1 glucose below 70 mg/dL and at or above 54; level 2 below 54 mg/dL; level 3 is a severe event with altered mental or physical status needing assistance, regardless of the number.
  • Symptoms: adrenergic (tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger) and neuroglycopenic (confusion, behavior change, seizure, focal deficits that mimic stroke, coma). Beta-blockers and hypoglycemia unawareness blunt the warning signs.
  • Causes: insulin or sulfonylurea therapy, reduced intake, renal failure (reduced insulin clearance), sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency, alcohol, insulinoma.

• Point-of-care glucose; confirm with a lab sample if it does not fit the picture, but treat first.
  • Before treatment in a patient without diabetes, if it will not delay care, draw blood for insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate and sulfonylurea screen to support later evaluation.
  • Look for the precipitant: renal function, infection, intake history, new medications, long-acting insulin or sulfonylurea exposure.

1. Able to swallow: the ADA 15-15 rule: 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat until resolved, then a meal or snack.
  2. Unable to swallow, no IV: glucagon. The FDA label for glucagon 1 mg/mL emergency kits gives 1 mg SC, IM, or IV for adults and children 6 years or older or above 25 kg, and 0.5 mg for children under 6 or under 25 kg, repeating once after 15 minutes if no response. ADA prefers ready-to-use products (intranasal or premixed) for out-of-hospital use.
  3. Unable to swallow, IV access: IV dextrose. The Hospira dextrose 50% label (revised January 2026) gives 10 to 25 g (20 to 50 mL of D50) slowly IV for adults and children 12 years and older, repeated as clinically needed. D10 delivers the same 10 to 25 g in 100 to 250 mL. The label advises against peripheral D50 in children 2 to 11 years (use central access or a lower concentration) and does not cover children under 2. In children, the OHSU dehydration pathway uses D10W 4 to 5 mL/kg (2 to 5 mL/kg in another section of the same pathway) with a recheck in 30 minutes.
  4. After correction: feed the patient, then start a dextrose infusion if hypoglycemia recurs or the cause is long-acting.
  5. Malnourished or alcohol-using patients: give thiamine with or before glucose.

Trap: Discharging a patient whose hypoglycemia came from a long-acting insulin, a sulfonylurea, or renal failure after one good glucose. These recur hours later, so observe with serial checks.
  • Glucagon works poorly when glycogen is depleted (starvation, alcohol, liver failure).
  • Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke; check glucose before activating a stroke pathway.
  • Patients with a clear, short-acting cause who eat and stay normal for several hours can often go home with a plan and glucagon; admit for recurrence, unclear cause, or poor intake.
  • Sulfonylurea or other drug-induced hypoglycemia after an overdose is a toxicology problem and outside this tab.

cards.q: What are ADA hypoglycemia levels 1, 2 and 3?
cards.a: Level 1 below 70 mg/dL (and 54 or above); level 2 below 54 mg/dL; level 3 is any event with altered status needing assistance.

cards.q: What is the ADA 15-15 rule?
cards.a: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck glucose in 15 minutes, and repeat until resolved.

cards.q: What adult IV dextrose dose does the D50 label give for insulin-induced hypoglycemia?
cards.a: 10 to 25 g (20 to 50 mL of 50% dextrose) slowly IV, repeated as needed; D10 gives the same grams in 100 to 250 mL.

cards.q: What glucagon doses does the FDA kit label give for severe hypoglycemia?
cards.a: 1 mg SC, IM, or IV for adults and children 6 years or older or over 25 kg; 0.5 mg if under 6 years or under 25 kg; repeat once after 15 minutes if no response.

cards.q: Which hypoglycemia causes require prolonged observation after correction?
cards.a: Long-acting insulin, sulfonylureas, renal failure, and poor intake, because recurrence is likely.

concepts.s: Protect the heart with IV calcium when the ECG shows toxicity, shift potassium into cells with insulin-glucose and salbutamol, remove it with binders or dialysis, and watch for rebound and hypoglycemia.

x.b:
• UK Kidney Association (UKKA) severity: mild 5.5 to 5.9, moderate 6.0 to 6.4, severe 6.5 mmol/L or higher.
  • Risk groups: CKD and dialysis, AKI, diabetes, heart failure on RAAS inhibitors, spironolactone, trimethoprim, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, adrenal insufficiency.
  • Symptoms are late: weakness, paresthesias, palpitations, ascending paralysis; arrest can be the first sign.
  • Pseudohyperkalemia: hemolysis, prolonged tourniquet, thrombocytosis or leukocytosis. Repeat, but treat if the ECG is abnormal.

• 12-lead ECG: UKKA recommends an urgent ECG for hospitalized patients with K 6.0 or higher. Look for peaked T waves, PR prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, bradycardia, sine wave, VF or asystole. A normal ECG does not exclude danger.
  • Cardiac monitoring (UKKA): K 6.5 or higher, any ECG changes, or K 6.0 to 6.4 if unwell or rising.
  • Blood gas for a fast potassium, creatinine, glucose, CK, calcium; review drugs.

Doses below are from the UKKA clinical practice guideline on management of hyperkalaemia in adults (2023, updated July 2026).

  1. Stabilize the myocardium (ECG changes): 6.8 mmol of calcium, as 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 10 minutes or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride over 5 minutes. Calcium chloride is preferred in arrest or peri-arrest. The July 2026 update downgraded IV calcium to a suggestion (2C) after a 2025 ILCOR review. UKKA advises a repeat dose if ECG changes persist, noting that calcium acts within 3 minutes but lasts only 30 to 60 minutes; it sets no fixed interval. The ACEP adult hyperkalemia algorithm gives calcium gluconate 1 g IV, rechecks the ECG at 5 minutes, and allows up to two further doses if changes persist.
  2. Shift: 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose IV for severe hyperkalemia (suggested for moderate). If pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) (126 mg/dL), follow with 10% glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 hours. Check glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 minutes. The ACEP algorithm uses 5 units of regular insulin in insulin-naive or CKD patients to lower hypoglycemia risk.
  3. Salbutamol (albuterol): 10 to 20 mg nebulized as an adjunct for severe hyperkalemia; never as monotherapy.
  4. Remove: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g three times daily for up to 72 hours for K 6.5 or higher (consider for 6.0 to 6.4); patiromer 8.4 g is an option at K 6.0 or higher. UKKA no longer recommends calcium resonium acutely.
  5. Sodium bicarbonate: UKKA does not recommend routine IV bicarbonate for acute treatment; it suggests it in cardiac arrest with suspected hyperkalemia.
  6. Dialysis: urgent for hemodialysis patients with K 6.5 or higher; still give IV calcium for ECG toxicity while dialysis is arranged.
  7. Fix the cause: stop potassium-raising drugs, treat AKI and obstruction, give fluids for hypovolemia.

Trap: Believing calcium or insulin lowers the body's potassium. Calcium only stabilizes membranes and insulin only shifts potassium; both wear off and the level rebounds without removal.
  • Insulin-glucose hypoglycemia is common and can be late; UKKA extended glucose monitoring to 6 hours.
  • Calcium gluconate underdosing: the UK MHRA 2023 alert led UKKA to specify 30 mL of 10% gluconate to match 10 mL of chloride.
  • UKKA suggests rechecking K at least at 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 hours after treating moderate or severe hyperkalemia.
  • Monitor in a high-dependency setting for severe or ECG-positive hyperkalemia; involve nephrology for refractory cases.

Raised extracellular potassium partially depolarizes cardiac cells, inactivating sodium channels and slowing conduction. Calcium raises the threshold potential and restores excitability; insulin and beta-agonists activate the sodium-potassium pump to move potassium inside.

cards.q: What IV calcium doses does UKKA give for hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride over 5 minutes (6.8 mmol); repeat if ECG changes persist (ACEP: recheck ECG at 5 minutes, up to two more doses).

cards.q: What insulin-glucose dose does UKKA recommend for severe hyperkalemia?
cards.a: 10 units soluble insulin with 25 g glucose IV.

cards.q: When does UKKA add a 10% glucose infusion after insulin-glucose?
cards.a: When pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL): 50 mL/h for 5 hours.

cards.q: What nebulized salbutamol dose does UKKA give as an adjunct?
cards.a: 10 to 20 mg.

cards.q: What UKKA potassium range defines severe hyperkalemia?
cards.a: 6.5 mmol/L or higher.

concepts.s: Treat severe symptomatic hyponatremia with 150 mL boluses of 3% saline to raise sodium about 5 mmol/L, then cap correction to protect against osmotic demyelination, and lower chronic hypernatremia gradually with free water.

x.b:
• Hyponatremia symptoms: nausea, headache, confusion, gait instability and falls; severe features are vomiting, seizures, reduced consciousness, and respiratory arrest. Acute drops (under 48 hours: marathon runners, psychogenic polydipsia, postoperative hypotonic fluids, MDMA) carry the highest risk of brain herniation.
  • High-risk for osmotic demyelination when corrected: sodium 105 or below, hypokalemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease.
  • Hypernatremia: usually loss of free water without access to water: infants, older or disabled patients, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis. Symptoms are lethargy, irritability, weakness, seizures; intracranial hemorrhage can result from brain shrinkage.

• Hyponatremia: serum osmolality (exclude isotonic pseudohyponatremia from lipids or protein and hypertonic hyponatremia from glucose or mannitol), urine osmolality, urine sodium, volume assessment, glucose, TSH, cortisol, medication review (thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine).
  • Glucose correction: WikEM cites a fall of about 1.6 mEq/L (Katz) or 2.4 mEq/L (Hillier) in measured sodium per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100.
  • Hypernatremia: urine osmolality and volume (dilute urine points to diabetes insipidus), glucose, calcium, potassium.
  • Free water deficit (WikEM): total body water times (Na/140 minus 1), with TBW about 0.6 of weight in men and 0.5 in women, less in older adults.

Hyponatremia (European 2014 guideline as summarized by WikEM, and the UK Society for Endocrinology 2022 emergency guidance):

  1. Severe symptoms: 150 mL of 3% saline IV over 20 minutes, recheck sodium, and repeat (the Society for Endocrinology 2022 guidance repeats twice, so up to 3 boluses) until symptoms improve or sodium has risen about 5 mmol/L. A UMEM summary of the University of Maryland protocol uses faster 150 mL boluses over 10 minutes for severe symptoms. Children: 2 mL/kg of 3% (WikEM).
  2. Moderately severe symptoms: one 150 mL bolus of 3% over 20 minutes, with sodium checks at 1, 6 and 12 hours.
  3. Correction limits: no more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each later 24 hours (European 2014); use a lower ceiling of about 8 mmol/L per day in high-risk patients. Society for Endocrinology 2022 stops hypertonic saline once the rise exceeds 10 mmol/L or sodium reaches 130 mmol/L, and advises against formula-based (Adrogue-Madias) dosing of hypertonic saline. Do not aim to normalize sodium on day one.
  4. Prevent or reverse overcorrection: desmopressin (WikEM cites 1 to 2 mcg IV every 6 to 8 hours) with or without free water, under specialist guidance.
  5. Mild or chronic, cause-directed: fluid restriction for SIADH, isotonic saline for hypovolemia (watch for brisk aquaresis once volume is restored), stop offending drugs, treat hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency.

Hypernatremia:

  1. Restore perfusion with isotonic fluid first if the patient is in shock.
  2. Then replace free water (enteral water, D5W, or hypotonic saline). WikEM gives a ceiling of about 10 to 12 mmol/L per 24 hours for chronic hypernatremia, while also quoting 10 to 15; acute hypernatremia (hours) can be corrected faster.
  3. Treat central diabetes insipidus with desmopressin; monitor sodium every few hours.

Trap: Overcorrection after the cause resolves. Once vasopressin falls (hypovolemia corrected, thiazide stopped, nausea treated), the kidneys can excrete liters of dilute urine and sodium can jump more than 10 mmol/L in hours. Track urine output and sodium every 2 to 4 hours.
  • Osmotic demyelination appears 2 to 6 days after overcorrection: dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, locked-in state.
  • Withholding 3% saline from a seizing patient out of fear of demyelination; acute cerebral edema kills faster.
  • Admit sodium below 120, any symptoms, and all hypertonic saline use to a monitored setting.

Water moves toward higher osmolality. Hyponatremia swells brain cells; over 48 hours the brain exports osmolytes to adapt, so chronic cases are less symptomatic but more vulnerable to rapid re-shrinking (demyelination) when sodium rises too fast.

cards.q: What is the initial 3% saline dose for severe symptomatic hyponatremia in the European 2014 approach?
cards.a: 150 mL IV over 20 minutes, repeated until symptoms improve or sodium rises about 5 mmol/L.

cards.q: What are the European 2014 correction limits for hyponatremia?
cards.a: No more than 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each subsequent 24 hours.

cards.q: Name four risk factors for osmotic demyelination.
cards.a: Sodium 105 or below, hypokalemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, and advanced liver disease.

cards.q: What is the free water deficit formula?
cards.a: Total body water (about 0.6 x weight in men, 0.5 in women) x (serum Na / 140 minus 1).

cards.q: What is a common correction ceiling for chronic hypernatremia?
cards.a: About 10 to 12 mmol/L per 24 hours (sources vary up to 15).

concepts.s: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately to any patient with known or suspected adrenal insufficiency who is in shock or vomiting, without waiting for a cortisol result.

x.b:
• Who: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia), pituitary disease, and most commonly glucocorticoid-induced suppression after long-term steroids; also adrenal hemorrhage (anticoagulation, meningococcemia), and checkpoint inhibitor hypophysitis.
  • Triggers: infection, gastroenteritis (cannot keep oral steroid down), surgery, trauma, missed doses.
  • Presentation: hypotension or shock refractory to fluids and pressors, vomiting, abdominal pain that mimics an acute abdomen, fever, confusion, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (primary only), hypoglycemia (especially children), and hyperpigmentation in chronic primary disease.

• Draw a random cortisol and ACTH (and renin if possible) before the first dose only if it causes no delay.
  • Electrolytes, glucose, creatinine, CBC, cultures, lactate, ECG for hyperkalemia.
  • Search for the precipitant: infection workup, imaging as indicated.
  • Formal stimulation testing waits until the patient is stable.

Doses below come from the UK Society for Endocrinology adrenal crisis emergency guidance.

  1. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.
  2. Then hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours, as a continuous IV infusion in 5% glucose or 50 mg IV or IM every 6 hours.
  3. Fluids: 500 mL of 0.9% saline over 15 minutes, then about 1 L per hour initially, with 3 to 4 L over 24 hours guided by response.
  4. Glucose: treat hypoglycemia.
  5. Children: the 2025 American Red Cross PALS septic shock card gives hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg IV or IO (maximum 100 mg) for children at risk of adrenal insufficiency who do not respond to fluids and vasopressors. The Endocrine Society 2016 primary adrenal insufficiency guideline gives 50 mg/m2 hydrocortisone as the first parenteral dose and 50 to 100 mg/m2 per 24 hours afterward.
  6. Mineralocorticoid: not needed acutely, because high-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity.
  7. Treat the trigger, then step down to oral steroids with endocrinology advice (Society for Endocrinology).

Trap: Waiting for a cortisol level or a stimulation test before giving steroids to a hypotensive patient. Hydrocortisone is safe and the crisis is lethal.
  • Dexamethasone does not cross-react with cortisol assays, but it provides no mineralocorticoid effect; hydrocortisone is the agent of choice.
  • Patients on chronic steroids may present with shock and no electrolyte clue because secondary insufficiency spares aldosterone.
  • Admit all adrenal crises; ICU for shock. Before discharge, teach sick-day rules, provide injectable hydrocortisone, and an emergency card.

cards.q: What is the first dose of hydrocortisone in adult adrenal crisis?
cards.a: 100 mg IV or IM immediately.

cards.q: What maintenance hydrocortisone dose follows the bolus in adults?
cards.a: 200 mg per 24 hours, as continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours.

cards.q: What pediatric hydrocortisone stress dose does the 2025 Red Cross PALS card give in shock at risk of adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: 2 mg/kg IV or IO, maximum 100 mg (the Endocrine Society 2016 guideline uses 50 mg/m2).

cards.q: Which electrolyte abnormality distinguishes primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia, because aldosterone is lost only in primary disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in ED patients?
cards.a: Suppression from long-term glucocorticoid therapy.

concepts.s: Thyroid storm is treated with beta-blockade, a thionamide, iodine given at least an hour after the thionamide, and steroids; myxedema coma is treated with IV levothyroxine, stress-dose hydrocortisone, and support of temperature, ventilation, and sodium.

x.b:
• Thyroid storm: thyrotoxicosis with decompensation: fever, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation out of proportion, heart failure, agitation, delirium or coma, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice. Triggers include infection, surgery, iodinated contrast, stopping antithyroid drugs, amiodarone, and pregnancy or delivery.
  • Myxedema coma: severe hypothyroidism with altered mentation, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation with hypercapnia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, and a precipitant (infection, cold exposure, sedatives, stopping levothyroxine); often an older woman in winter.
  • Mimics: sepsis, sympathomimetic toxicity, heat stroke, adrenal crisis.

• TSH, free T4 (and T3 in storm), but treat on clinical grounds.
  • Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale for storm: per the Vanderbilt Vim Book, a score of 45 or more is highly suggestive, 25 to 44 suggests impending storm, under 25 unlikely.
  • Myxedema coma screening tool (Emergency Care BC summary): scores GCS, TSH, free T4, temperature below 35 C, heart rate below 60, and a precipitant; 8 to 10 is most likely, 5 to 7 likely. It is based on low-quality evidence.
  • Cortisol, glucose, sodium, blood gas, ECG, cultures, troponin, echo for heart failure in storm.

Thyroid storm (doses as listed by LITFL and the Vanderbilt Vim Book; a 2026 JCEM review by Kopp and colleagues covers the approach):

  1. Beta-blockade: propranolol 60 to 80 mg PO every 4 hours, or esmolol 250 to 500 mcg/kg IV load then 50 to 200 mcg/kg/min when titratability matters. Avoid or use cautiously in decompensated heart failure or shock.
  2. Thionamide: propylthiouracil 500 to 1000 mg load, then 250 mg every 4 hours (PO, NG, or rectal), or methimazole 20 mg every 4 to 6 hours (60 to 80 mg per day in an Emory summary of ATA/AACE guidance). PTU also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
  3. Iodine at least 1 hour after the thionamide: Lugol's solution 0.5 mL (10 drops) every 6 to 8 hours per LITFL, or 8 drops (0.4 mL) every 6 hours per the Vim Book; SSKI 5 drops every 6 hours is the alternative in the Emory ATA/AACE summary.
  4. Hydrocortisone 300 mg IV load, then 100 mg IV every 8 hours.
  5. Adjuncts: cholestyramine 4 g PO every 8 hours (LITFL), active cooling, acetaminophen rather than aspirin, treat the trigger; plasmapheresis for refractory cases.

Myxedema coma (Emergency Care BC):

  1. Hydrocortisone 100 to 200 mg IV every 8 hours until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, given with or before thyroid hormone.
  2. Levothyroxine IV load 4 mcg/kg (about 200 to 400 mcg); 100 mcg if elderly, small, or with coronary disease or arrhythmia. Then 100 mcg IV at 24 hours and 50 mcg IV daily until oral intake.
  3. Liothyronine (T3) as an adjunct for persistent instability: 5 to 20 mcg IV load (5 to 10 mcg if elderly, small, or with coronary disease or arrhythmia), then 2.5 to 10 mcg every 8 hours.
  4. Support: intubate for hypoventilation, passive rewarming (active rewarming can provoke vasodilatory hypotension), gentle fluids, vasopressors if needed, treat hyponatremia and hypoglycemia, find the precipitant.

Trap: Giving iodine before the thionamide in thyroid storm. Iodine given first can supply substrate for more hormone synthesis.
  • Beta-blocking a storm patient in high-output heart failure or cardiogenic shock can precipitate collapse; esmolol allows quick reversal.
  • Missing coexisting adrenal insufficiency; give hydrocortisone in both conditions.
  • In myxedema coma, sedatives and opioids can stop respiration; drug metabolism is slowed.
  • Both conditions need ICU admission and early endocrinology involvement.

cards.q: In thyroid storm, how long after the thionamide should iodine be given?
cards.a: At least 1 hour.

cards.q: What PTU loading and maintenance doses are used in thyroid storm?
cards.a: 500 to 1000 mg load, then 250 mg every 4 hours.

cards.q: What Burch-Wartofsky score is highly suggestive of thyroid storm?
cards.a: 45 or more.

cards.q: What IV levothyroxine loading dose is used in myxedema coma?
cards.a: About 4 mcg/kg (200 to 400 mcg), or 100 mcg in elderly or cardiac patients.

cards.q: Why give hydrocortisone in myxedema coma before thyroid hormone?
cards.a: Coexisting adrenal insufficiency is possible, and thyroid hormone raises cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

concepts.n: Upper GI bleeding, including variceal hemorrhage
concepts.s: Resuscitate with a restrictive transfusion threshold, risk stratify with Glasgow-Blatchford, scope within 24 hours, and treat suspected varices with a vasoactive drug, ceftriaxone, and endoscopy within 12 hours.

x.b:
• Presentation: hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena; brisk upper bleeding can cause hematochezia with hemodynamic instability.
  • Causes: peptic ulcer (NSAIDs, aspirin, H. pylori, anticoagulants), varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophagitis, malignancy, Dieulafoy lesion, aortoenteric fistula after aortic graft.
  • Suspect varices with known cirrhosis, stigmata of liver disease, alcohol use, or thrombocytopenia.
  • Red flags: syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, ongoing hematemesis, rising BUN to creatinine ratio, age, cardiac disease.

• CBC (initial hemoglobin may be falsely reassuring), type and crossmatch, BUN, creatinine, LFTs, INR, lactate.
  • Glasgow-Blatchford score (GBS) uses BUN, hemoglobin (sex-specific), systolic BP, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease and cardiac failure. The 2021 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guideline suggests discharge with outpatient follow-up for very-low-risk patients, such as GBS 0 to 1. ACG chose this cutoff for about 99 percent sensitivity (false-negative rate 1 percent or less); specificity of GBS 0 to 1 is only about 27 to 40 percent.
  • NG lavage is not needed for diagnosis. CT angiography helps when bleeding is massive and endoscopy is delayed or nondiagnostic.

Nonvariceal bleeding (ACG 2021 upper GI and ulcer bleeding guideline):

  1. Airway protection for massive hematemesis or altered mentation.
  2. Restrictive transfusion at hemoglobin below 7 g/dL; ACG considers 8 g/dL reasonable with cardiovascular disease, and hypotensive patients may need blood at higher levels.
  3. Erythromycin 250 mg IV given 20 to 90 minutes before endoscopy (conditional) improves visualization.
  4. PPI before endoscopy: ACG 2021 makes no recommendation for or against; many centers still give it.
  5. Endoscopy within 24 hours for admitted patients.
  6. After endoscopic hemostasis: high-dose PPI for 3 days: 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h infusion for 72 hours, or intermittent dosing of an 80 mg bolus then 40 mg 2 to 4 times daily; then twice-daily PPI through 2 weeks for high-risk ulcers.
  7. Anticoagulation: reverse based on agent and severity with the GI team and cardiology.

Suspected variceal bleeding (Baveno VII as summarized in Spanish hepatology teaching slides, and a 2024 Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine review):

  1. Vasoactive drug started before endoscopy: octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus (the slides list 50 to 100 mcg), then 50 mcg/h, continued for 2 to 5 days. Terlipressin is an alternative where available.
  2. Antibiotic prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours; the 2024 CCJM review gives 5 days, and the teaching slides cite 7 days from the original trial.
  3. Restrictive transfusion at hemoglobin 7 g/dL with a target of 7 to 8 g/dL (CCJM 2024, consistent with Baveno VII); avoid plasma and platelets to correct INR or counts, which add volume; over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.
  4. Endoscopy within 12 hours of presentation once resuscitated, sooner if unstable; band ligation is preferred.
  5. Preemptive TIPS within 72 hours (ideally 24) for high-risk patients: Child-Pugh C 10 to 13 points, or Child-Pugh B with active bleeding at endoscopy (Baveno VII uses B above 7 points; the CCJM review uses B 7 to 9).
  6. Rescue: balloon tamponade or an esophageal stent as a bridge (tamponade 24 to 48 hours maximum, requires intubation), then TIPS.

Trap: Liberal transfusion in variceal bleeding. Driving hemoglobin high raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding and mortality.
  • A normal first hemoglobin in a hypotensive patient: equilibration has not happened yet.
  • Forgetting antibiotics in cirrhotic bleeds; infection is common and prophylaxis lowers mortality.
  • Missing aortoenteric fistula in a patient with an aortic graft and a herald bleed; get CT angiography and vascular surgery.
  • Disposition: GBS 0 to 1 can be discharged with follow-up; varices, instability, ongoing bleeding, or transfusion need admission, often ICU.

cards.q: Per ACG 2021, which Glasgow-Blatchford scores allow ED discharge for upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Very-low-risk patients such as GBS 0 to 1.

cards.q: What transfusion threshold does ACG 2021 recommend in upper GI bleeding?
cards.a: Hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, with 8 g/dL reasonable in cardiovascular disease; in variceal bleeding the target is 7 to 8 g/dL.

cards.q: What is the high-dose PPI regimen after endoscopic hemostasis per ACG 2021?
cards.a: 80 mg IV bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 hours, or an 80 mg bolus then 40 mg 2 to 4 times daily for 3 days.

cards.q: What is the octreotide regimen for variceal bleeding?
cards.a: 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/h for 2 to 5 days.

cards.q: What antibiotic and endoscopy timing apply to suspected variceal bleeding?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (5 to 7 days) and endoscopy within 12 hours.

concepts.s: Most lower GI bleeding stops on its own, so resuscitate, exclude an upper source when the patient is unstable, get CT angiography for hemodynamically significant bleeding, and schedule colonoscopy rather than rushing it.

x.b:
• Presentation: hematochezia or maroon stool; melena suggests a proximal source.
  • Causes: diverticular bleeding (painless, large volume, often older patients), angiodysplasia, ischemic colitis (pain then bloody diarrhea), post-polypectomy bleeding, hemorrhoids, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, infectious colitis.
  • Hematochezia with shock can be a brisk upper GI bleed; a high BUN to creatinine ratio and hemodynamic instability point upward.

• CBC, type and screen, coagulation, BUN, creatinine; rectal exam.
  • Risk stratification: the 2023 ACG lower GI bleeding guideline (as summarized in AFP) states the Oakland score can help identify patients who may not need admission, with clinical judgment taking priority. An AFP 2025 evidence summary gives an Oakland score of 8 or less as the threshold for safe discharge.
  • CT angiography for hemodynamically significant bleeding, with about 90 percent sensitivity; about 80 percent of patients with a negative CTA do not rebleed.
  • Upper endoscopy first when hematochezia comes with instability or upper GI features.

Recommendations below are from the 2023 ACG guideline as summarized by AFP (2024).

  1. Resuscitation with crystalloid and blood.
  2. Transfusion: restrictive threshold of hemoglobin below 7 g/dL in stable patients; consider 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or ACS.
  3. Positive CTA: transcatheter angiography with embolization, ideally within 90 minutes.
  4. Colonoscopy: the standard test in stable patients, usually inpatient or within 14 days of spontaneous hemostasis; urgent colonoscopy within 24 hours did not improve outcomes.
  5. Antithrombotics: avoid reversal unless instability persists despite resuscitation; endoscopy is generally safe with INR up to 2.5; platelet targets above 30,000 in severe bleeding and above 50,000 for endoscopic procedures.
  6. Avoid tranexamic acid: it increases thrombosis without benefit in lower GI bleeding.
  7. Surgery is reserved for refractory bleeding after embolization or endoscopy fails.

Trap: Calling hematochezia with shock a lower bleed and skipping the upper endoscopy. A brisk upper GI source can present this way.
  • Restart aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention after bleeding stops; stop aspirin taken for primary prevention and NSAIDs after a diverticular bleed (ACG 2023).
  • Older patients on anticoagulants with recurrent bleeding need admission even when vital signs are normal.
  • Ischemic colitis with peritonitis or a right-sided pattern can signal mesenteric ischemia.

cards.q: Which imaging test does ACG 2023 favor for hemodynamically significant lower GI bleeding?
cards.a: CT angiography (about 90 percent sensitive).

cards.q: Within what time should angiographic embolization follow a positive CTA?
cards.a: Within about 90 minutes.

cards.q: What Oakland score identifies lower GI bleeding patients suitable for discharge?
cards.a: 8 or less (AFP 2025 summary), with clinical judgment taking priority per ACG 2023.

cards.q: Should tranexamic acid be used in lower GI bleeding per ACG 2023?
cards.a: No; it raises thromboembolism and seizure risk without benefit.

cards.q: What must be excluded in hematochezia with hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: A brisk upper GI bleeding source, by upper endoscopy.

concepts.n: Acute abdomen: appendicitis, bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischemia, AAA
concepts.s: Pain out of proportion, peritonitis, shock, or age over 50 with abdominal pain demands early imaging and surgery, because mesenteric ischemia, ruptured AAA, perforation, and strangulated obstruction kill quickly.

x.b:
• Red flags: sudden severe pain, pain out of proportion to exam, peritonitis (rigidity, rebound), syncope or hypotension, older age, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, atrial fibrillation.
  • Appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea, fever, leukocytosis; atypical in pregnancy, older adults and young children.
  • Small bowel obstruction: colicky pain, distension, vomiting, obstipation; prior surgery (adhesions) or hernia. Fever, constant pain, tachycardia, peritonism and lactate suggest strangulation.
  • Acute mesenteric ischemia: severe pain with a soft abdomen early, often with atrial fibrillation (embolic), atherosclerosis (thrombotic), low-flow states (nonocclusive), or hypercoagulability (venous).
  • Abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture: abdominal, back or flank pain with syncope or hypotension; often misdiagnosed as renal colic in older men.

• Appendicitis (WSES Jerusalem guidelines 2020 update): clinical scores exclude appendicitis and identify intermediate-risk patients for imaging; the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response (AIR) and Adult Appendicitis Score (AAS) perform best in adults, and Alvarado is not specific enough to confirm the diagnosis. Point-of-care ultrasound is the preferred first imaging test in adults and children; low-dose CT is preferred over standard-dose in adolescents and young adults with negative ultrasound; in pregnancy use ultrasound then MRI; in children avoid routine first-line CT.
  • Bowel obstruction: CT with IV contrast identifies the transition point, closed loop, and ischemia signs (reduced wall enhancement, pneumatosis, mesenteric fluid, whirl sign).
  • Mesenteric ischemia: biphasic CT angiography without oral contrast immediately, even with AKI (McMaster Textbook of Internal Medicine, citing WSES 2022). Lactate and D-dimer rise late and lack specificity; a normal lactate does not exclude it.
  • AAA: bedside ultrasound of the aorta (an aorta 3 cm or larger is aneurysmal); CT angiography if stable. ESVS 2024 sets elective repair thresholds of 5.5 cm in men and 5.0 cm in women.

1. All: resuscitate, analgesia (opioids do not mask diagnosis), NPO, early surgical consultation.
  2. Appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy is standard; WSES 2020 supports antibiotic-first nonoperative management as an option for selected uncomplicated cases after shared decision-making. Give preoperative antibiotics.
  3. Adhesive small bowel obstruction: nasogastric decompression, fluids, electrolyte correction, and a trial of nonoperative management if no strangulation; water-soluble contrast challenge has diagnostic and therapeutic value (WSES Bologna 2013 update: 50 to 150 mL Gastrografin orally or by NG tube; contrast in the colon on an abdominal film within 24 hours predicts resolution; operate after 72 hours of nonoperative management without resolution). Immediate surgery for peritonitis, strangulation, closed loop, or failure to progress.
  4. Mesenteric ischemia: unfractionated heparin by continuous infusion unless contraindicated (WSES 2022, grade 1B; neither WSES 2022 nor the ESVS 2017 mesenteric guideline gives a bolus or infusion rate, so use the institutional weight-based therapeutic heparin nomogram), broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergent revascularization (endovascular or open) plus resection of nonviable bowel with a planned second look. Venous thrombosis without necrosis may respond to anticoagulation alone.
  5. Ruptured AAA: immediate vascular surgery, massive transfusion activation, permissive hypotension (ESVS 2024 class I: target systolic pressure 70 to 90 mmHg as long as the patient stays conscious, with ability to speak as the marker of cerebral perfusion), local anesthesia for EVAR whenever tolerated,, and EVAR as the first-line repair when anatomy allows (ESVS 2024 class I, level A).

Trap: Diagnosing renal colic in an older patient with flank pain and hematuria without looking at the aorta. Bedside ultrasound takes a minute.
  • A soft abdomen with severe pain in a patient with atrial fibrillation is mesenteric ischemia until CTA says otherwise.
  • Older adults and immunosuppressed patients may have perforation or ischemia without fever, leukocytosis, or peritonism.
  • Reassess abdominal pain sent home: give strict return precautions and a planned recheck when the diagnosis is uncertain.

cards.q: Which appendicitis scores does WSES 2020 recommend as best predictors in adults?
cards.a: The AIR (Appendicitis Inflammatory Response) and AAS (Adult Appendicitis Score).

cards.q: What permissive hypotension target does ESVS 2024 give for ruptured AAA?
cards.a: Systolic pressure 70 to 90 mmHg while the patient remains conscious and able to speak.

cards.q: What imaging is needed immediately for suspected mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Biphasic CT angiography without oral contrast, even with AKI.

cards.q: What anticoagulant is recommended first in occlusive mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Continuous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated.

cards.q: What is the first-line repair for ruptured AAA in ESVS 2024 when anatomy allows?
cards.a: EVAR (class I, level A).

concepts.s: Diagnose with two of three criteria, give moderate lactated Ringer's resuscitation rather than aggressive fluids, feed early, skip prophylactic antibiotics, and reserve urgent ERCP for cholangitis.

x.b:
• Presentation: severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting; Cullen and Grey Turner signs are late markers of hemorrhage.
  • Causes: gallstones and alcohol most often; hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, post-ERCP, drugs, trauma, tumors.
  • Severity (revised Atlanta classification): mild (no organ failure or local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure under 48 hours or local complications), severe (persistent organ failure over 48 hours).
  • Differential: perforated ulcer, mesenteric ischemia, AAA, biliary disease, inferior MI.

• Diagnosis (revised Atlanta): two of three: typical pain, lipase or amylase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic imaging. Lipase level does not track severity.
  • Ultrasound to look for gallstones; ACG 2024 suggests repeating it if the first is inconclusive.
  • CT only if the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient worsens; early CT underestimates necrosis.
  • Labs: CBC, BUN, creatinine, LFTs, calcium, triglycerides, lactate. Trend BUN, hematocrit, and urine output to judge resuscitation.

From the 2024 ACG acute pancreatitis guideline (Tenner and colleagues):

  1. Fluids: moderately aggressive resuscitation, adding boluses only if hypovolemic; lactated Ringer's over normal saline. The WATERFALL trial (NEJM 2022) that informed this used a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h; the aggressive arm (20 mL/kg then 3 mL/kg/h) caused more fluid overload without benefit and was stopped early.
